procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 15.12.2009 convicting the petitioner under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and sentencing them to undergo imprisonment for life.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner appealed the Sessions Court's judgment to the High Court of Andhra Pradesh, which dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction by its judgment dated 10.04.2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) against the concurrent findings of the Sessions Court and the High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the SLP on 12.07.2022, finalizing the conviction and sentence. Two months after the dismissal of the SLP, the petitioner filed a Writ Petition praying that a Writ of Mandamus be issued to the State to verify his claim of juvenility and to pass necessary consequential orders.

directions: The petitioner be released forthwith, if he is not required to be detained in any other case.
There shall be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's claim of juvenility, raised after his conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC, should be accepted.

facts: The petitioner was convicted under Section 302 r/w Section 34 of the IPC for a crime committed on 21.12.2005 and sentenced to life imprisonment.
His conviction and sentence were upheld by the High Court, and his Special Leave Petition (SLP) was dismissed by the Supreme Court, making the conviction final.
After the dismissal of his SLP, the petitioner filed a Writ Petition claiming he was a juvenile at the time of the offense.
The Supreme Court ordered an enquiry, and an Additional Sessions Judge submitted a report based on school records and witness testimony.
The report concluded that the petitioner's date of birth was 02.05.1989, making him 16 years and 7 months old on the date of the crime.
By the time of the hearing, the petitioner had already been imprisoned for more than 12 years.
law: Under Section 7A(1) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, a claim of juvenility can be raised before any court and at any stage.
Under Section 16 read with Section 15(1)(g) of the same Act, the maximum period of incarceration for a juvenile in conflict with the law is three years.
application: The Court first affirmed its jurisdiction to hear the plea, as Section 7A(1) of the Juvenile Justice Act allows the claim to be raised at any time, even after a conviction has become final.

The Court accepted the factual findings of the enquiry report from the Additional Sessions Judge, which confirmed the petitioner's date of birth and established his status as a juvenile at the time of the offense.

The Court then applied the maximum punishment provision from the Juvenile Justice Act. It noted that the petitioner had already served over 12 years in prison, which is significantly more than the three-year maximum sentence permitted for a juvenile.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's claim of juvenility. Because he had already served much more than the maximum statutory punishment of three years under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, the Court held that he could no longer be incarcerated and directed his immediate release.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's claim of juvenility, raised after his conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC, should be accepted.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner filed a Writ Petition praying that a Writ of Mandamus be issued to the State to verify his claim of juvenility and to pass necessary consequential orders, even though this claim was raised after his conviction was upheld by the High Court and his Special Leave Petition was dismissed by the Supreme Court.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not contain the arguments made by the respondent.

statutes.act_name: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000

cases.case_name: Hari Ram v. State of Rajasthan & Anr.
cases.principle: A plea of juvenility can be raised at any stage of the proceedings.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A plea of juvenility can be raised at any stage, even after a conviction has attained finality. If the claim is verified, the convicted person is entitled to the benefits of the Juvenile Justice Act, and any sentence imposed beyond the maximum statutory punishment prescribed by that Act is unsustainable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's core finding was that the petitioner's claim of juvenility was factually correct and legally dispositive, mandating his immediate release. The court's reasoning proceeded in steps: first, it accepted the factual report of the Additional Sessions Judge, which conclusively established the petitioner's date of birth as 02.05.1989, making him 16 years and 7 months old on the date of the offense. Second, applying the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, the court determined that the maximum sentence the petitioner could have legally served was three years. Finally, given that the petitioner had already been incarcerated for over 12 years—a period far exceeding the statutory maximum—the court concluded that his continued detention was unlawful.
legal_tests_applied: A plea of juvenility can be raised at any stage.
Under Section 16 read with Section 15(1)(g) of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, the maximum period of custody for a juvenile is three years.
policy_considerations: The court's action upholds the fundamental policy of juvenile justice that the special protections for juveniles are paramount and can be invoked at any point in the legal process, even after a conviction has been finalized by the highest courts. By stating, "As such a plea can be raised at any stage, we called for a report after due enquiry," the court reinforces the principle that the legal status of being a juvenile at the time of an offense is a non-waivable right that overrides procedural finality.
